title: Chapter 29 — The Kitchen Package Sale
intro: The highest-ticket sale on the retail floor — recognizing the opportunity, building the package, and coordinating a multi-product purchase.

sections.title: Recognizing the Package Opportunity
sections.content:
A kitchen package sale does not always announce itself. The customer who walks in asking about a refrigerator may also need a range, a dishwasher, a microwave, and ventilation. But they will not volunteer that unless you ask.

This is where discovery earns its keep. The question 'Tell me about your kitchen' is not casual conversation. It is the question that turns a $2,000 refrigerator sale into a $15,000 kitchen package.

Customers doing a renovation are especially likely to buy everything at once — but only if someone helps them think through the full picture. Most customers have never bought an entire kitchen before. They need guidance. They need someone to coordinate it.

sections.title: Build the Package Logically
sections.content:
Do not try to sell five appliances in five separate conversations. Build the package as one coordinated solution.

Start with the anchor — usually the refrigerator or the range, whichever the customer mentioned first. Then expand naturally. 'Now that we have the fridge sorted, let us make sure the rest of the kitchen works together. Are you planning to update the range at the same time?'

Match brands where appropriate. Coordinate finishes. Check compatibility. Help them see the kitchen as a system, not a collection of individual purchases.

The customer should feel like they are designing their kitchen — not being upsold five times.

sections.title: Coordination Is the Skill
sections.content:
A kitchen package involves delivery timing, installation scheduling, contractor coordination, electrical and plumbing requirements, ventilation planning, and sometimes cabinet modifications.

The salesperson who can coordinate all of this becomes indispensable. You are no longer just selling appliances. You are managing a project. That is a completely different level of value — and customers will pay for it, refer you for it, and come back to you because of it.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating kitchen package selling, ask:

Does the salesperson recognize package opportunities during discovery — or only sell what the customer specifically asked about?
Do they build the package as a coordinated solution — or pitch each appliance separately?
Can they manage the logistics — delivery, installation, compatibility, timing?
Does the customer feel guided through a complex purchase — or overwhelmed by it?

The kitchen package is the highest-ticket sale on the floor. The salesperson who masters it earns disproportionately more than the one who only sells single appliances.
